reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: A group of type II CDGs caused by defects in subunits of the conserved oligomeric Golgi (COG) complex, which maintains Golgi structure and glycosyltransferase localisation
Presents with developmental delay, hypotonia, microcephaly, failure to thrive and variable dysmorphism, with severity depending on the affected subunit
Hepatic involvement, feeding difficulty and recurrent infections are common; some subunits (e.g. COG7) cause a severe neonatal presentation with fatal outcome
Skin findings, thermal dysregulation and gastrointestinal problems are reported in certain subtypes
Because COG dysfunction disturbs multiple Golgi glycosyltransferases, transferrin shows a type II pattern, and both N- and O-glycosylation may be affected
Management is supportive and multidisciplinary; no specific therapy corrects the trafficking defect
Diagnosis requires molecular testing of the relevant COG subunit gene after a type II transferrin pattern
reference.pathophysiology: The conserved oligomeric Golgi complex is a multisubunit tethering complex that maintains Golgi architecture and the correct positioning and retrieval of glycosylation enzymes. Defects in COG subunits mislocalise multiple glycosyltransferases and disrupt intra-Golgi trafficking, impairing the processing of both N- and O-linked glycans. Because the defect lies in Golgi processing rather than precursor assembly, transferrin shows a type II pattern. The breadth of affected glycoproteins accounts for the multisystem phenotype, and the specific subunit affected influences severity.
additionalDifferentials: Other type II CDG subtypes (e.g. MGAT2-CDG, TMEM165-CDG, B4GALT1-CDG, SLC35A2-CDG)
Other Golgi trafficking and vesicular transport disorders
Syndromic causes of microcephaly with failure to thrive
Type I CDGs when the transferrin pattern is ambiguous
additionalInvestigations: Transferrin isoelectric focusing or mass spectrometry showing a type II pattern
Molecular testing of the relevant COG subunit gene (COG1 through COG8)
Analysis of O-glycosylation (e.g. apolipoprotein C-III) where available
redFlags: Severe neonatal presentation with rapid deterioration (notably some COG7 cases)
Failure to thrive with multi-organ involvement
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies widely by subunit and severity, from lethal neonatal forms to milder presentations with survival and moderate disability; outcome is dominated by hepatic, infective and neurological complications. No corrective treatment exists.
pitfalls: Stopping at a type II transferrin result without identifying the specific COG subunit
Overlooking abnormal O-glycosylation, which can help characterise COG defects
Not anticipating infection and hepatic risk
Assuming a uniform prognosis across the COG-complex group
references: Scriver's OMMBID, congenital disorders of glycosylation
Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics, disorders of glycosylation
management: No corrective therapy addresses the trafficking defect; management is supportive and multidisciplinary and tailored to the affected subunit
Nutritional and feeding support for failure to thrive and hypotonia, with tube feeding where needed
Hepatic surveillance and management of liver involvement, including coagulation support
Prompt treatment of recurrent infections with immune assessment, and management of thermal dysregulation and gastrointestinal problems in affected subtypes
Developmental support and neuroimaging-guided care for neurological manifestations, with anticonvulsants for seizures
Monitoring of hepatic, immune and neurological status across the multisystem disease
Genetic counselling for these autosomal recessive COG-subunit disorders, with cascade family testing and prenatal options
Escalate severe neonatal presentations such as COG7 for intensive supportive care given the risk of early death
